entry.gloss: notes in step order from a note to its octave
entry.def: A series of notes in step order, rising or falling from a starting note to its octave, with a fixed pattern of whole steps and half steps. The pattern gives the scale its type, such as major or minor.

The seven-note scale with the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half step, so its half steps lie between the third and fourth and the seventh and eighth degrees. On the white keys of the piano it runs from C to C.

figure.caption: The C major scale: half steps between 3 and 4 and between 7 and 8.

entry.def: The minor scale with the pattern whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole step; its half steps lie between degrees 2 and 3 and degrees 5 and 6. It has the same notes as its relative major scale, starting on that scale's sixth degree. Also called the Aeolian mode.

entry.gloss: natural minor with a raised seventh
entry.def: The natural minor scale with its seventh degree raised by a half step, which gives the minor key a leading tone. The raised seventh leaves an augmented second, three half steps, between the sixth and seventh degrees.

figure.staff: A4 B4 C5 D5 E5 F5 *G#5 A5
figure.caption: The A harmonic minor scale, with G# as its raised seventh.

entry.gloss: raised sixth and seventh going up, natural minor going down
entry.def: A minor scale whose sixth and seventh degrees are raised on the way up, avoiding the augmented second of the harmonic minor, and which descends as the natural minor scale. In jazz the raised form is used in both directions.

figure.staff: A4 B4 C5 D5 E5 *F#5 *G#5 A5 *G5 *F5 E5 D5 C5 B4 A4
figure.caption: The A melodic minor scale, up and down.

entry.gloss: all twelve notes, in half steps
entry.def: A scale made only of half steps, using all twelve notes of the octave. It is usually written with sharps going up and flats going down.

figure.staff: C4 C#4 D4 D#4 E4 F4 F#4 G4 G#4 A4 A#4 B4 C5

entry.gloss: the home note and scale a piece is built on
entry.def: The tonic and the scale that a piece or passage is based on: music in G major uses the notes of the G major scale and treats G as its home. The key signature shows the key's sharps or flats.

entry.gloss: sharps or flats at the start of every staff
entry.def: The sharps or flats written after the clef at the start of every staff. They apply to every note with those letter names, in every octave, unless an accidental cancels them. Each key signature belongs to one major key and its relative minor.

figure.caption: Three flats: the key signature of Eb major and C minor.

entry.gloss: each new sharp a fifth above the last
entry.def: Sharps always appear in a key signature in the same order, each a fifth above the one before: F# C# G# D# A# E# B#. The last sharp is the leading tone of the major key, a half step below its tonic.

entry.gloss: each new flat a fifth below the last
entry.def: Flats always appear in a key signature in the same order, each a fifth below the one before: Bb Eb Ab Db Gb Cb Fb, the order of sharps backwards. With two or more flats, the second-to-last flat names the major key.

entry.gloss: the keys arranged in a circle a fifth apart
entry.def: The keys arranged in a circle: going clockwise from C major, each key's tonic is a perfect fifth higher and its signature has one more sharp or one fewer flat. The sharp and flat keys meet at the bottom, where three pairs of keys are enharmonic.

entry.gloss: major and minor keys that share a key signature
entry.def: A major key and a minor key with the same key signature, such as C major and A minor. The tonic of the relative minor is the sixth degree of the major key, a minor third below the major tonic.

entry.gloss: major and minor keys with the same tonic
entry.def: A major key and a minor key with the same tonic, such as C major and C minor. Their key signatures differ by three accidentals: C major has none and C minor has three flats. Called the tonic major or tonic minor in British English.

entry.gloss: using only the notes of the key
entry.def: Belonging to the key: using only the seven notes of its scale, without added accidentals. The opposite of chromatic.
